2284.prule: No word stress: the source states that stress 'in the classical sense' is absent in Guro. Guro is a tone language with five tonemes (high, mid, low, rising, falling), tone-bearing unit = syllable. Within the (maximally disyllabic) phonological foot there is a structure-dependent, non-phonological weakening of one syllable (first vowel reduces or deletes in CVLV feet with identical vowels; in southern dialects the second syllable's initial consonant may drop; some feet show neither), which the authors say has no phonological significance but could in future develop into word and syntagmatic stress. At syntagm level the rhythmic peak (syntactic head word or last word of the group) is phonetically marked by intensity and vowel duration.

2284.tone: Five phonological tonemes (H, M, L, rising, falling), TBU = syllable, with lexical and grammatical functions (p. 770, Table 5). On stress the source says it is absent 'in the classical sense'; the only prominence asymmetry is a non-phonological, segmentally predictable weakening of one syllable inside the disyllabic foot, plus a syntagm-level rhythmic peak (intensity + duration) on the head or final word. Earlier literature: Vydrine 2003 (Mandenkan 38, sec. 3 and Conclusions) proposed, explicitly as 'observations préliminaires', an 'accent dynamique' (intensity + vowel length) whose placement is 'partiellement déterminé' by the vowel combination in the foot: 2nd syllable in CVLV feet with identical vowels, 1st syllable when V1 is more open than V2, plus a class of 'mots sans accent'; phrase accent unstudied. Kuznetsova 2007 (Mandenkan 43: 41-42) rejects this: 'la notion d'accent phonologique n'est pas très fonctionnelle pour le gouro', reduction is predictable from segmental structure, no minimal pairs by accent are possible; a phonetic-level inequality resembling lexical and syntagmatic accent is emerging. The 2017 chapter (Kuznetsova & Kuznetsova, in a volume edited by Vydrin) restates the no-stress position.

2287.prule: Main (expiratory) stress falls as a rule on the root syllable: in simplex words on the root syllable (= the initial syllable of native unprefixed words), in compounds on the root syllable of the first member. Position is set by morpheme class: prefixes be-, of-, æm-, most for- 'ver-', many and-, mis-, o-/u- 'un-', unt- and many compounds (especially verbs) with the particles a, af, bort, fram, in, til, um, up, ut, væl leave main stress on the second member; loan suffixes -era/-inna/-issa attract penultimate and -eri/-ær final main stress; -ing/-ung derivatives alternately suffix-stressed; a listed residue of single words and loans has non-root stress. Weight plays no role in main-stress placement.
2287.srule: Four degrees (main, strong secondary, weak secondary, unstressed). Strong secondary stress: in compounds on the root syllable of the non-main-stressed member (suffixed article always weak/unstressed; obscured compounds sink to weak); in simplex words on the syllable immediately after a short stem syllable (svarabhakti vowels and clitic-prone disyllables excepted; later reduced to weak), and after a long stem syllable only on the derivational syllables -ind-, -ine, -ing-, -isk-, -ist-, -und-, -ung-, -ærne (most -tan numerals; -and-/-ast- fluctuate) and in single words. Weak secondary stress: regularly on the syllable after a long stem syllable in simplex words, absent on svarabhakti vowels, in disyllabic comparatives, clitic-prone words, and when an unstressed prefix or proclitic precedes the main stress. Stated for Old Swedish; Old Gutnish covered by the grammar's scope only.

2288.dq: All Gwandara dialects have three level tones, high, mid and low. (The statement concerns lexical tone on citation forms in a comparative wordlist; no word- or phrase-level stress/prominence is described anywhere in the Introduction, pp. 11-26.)
2288.prule: No word-stress or accent rule is stated anywhere in the reachable descriptions. Gwandara is described as a three-level tone language (high, mid, low) with three rising and three falling contour tones plus rare rising-falling / falling-rising contours; a contour-bearing syllable is phonetically longer than a level-tone syllable; the reference dialect (Karshi) has no phonemic vowel length (Gitata dialect does, sec. 0.6.4).
2288.srule: Not mentioned in Matsushita 1974 (Introduction secs. 0.1-0.7, pp. 11-26 read; sec. 0.5 describes tone notation only: three level tones H/M/L plus contours, no stress, accent or rhythm statement).
2288.quote: All Gwandara dialects have three level tones, high, mid and low. Kar: /tá/ (high) 'to keep on' /da/ (mid) 'one' /tà/ (low) 'to go to' Three rising tones (mid to high, low to high, low to mid) and three falling tones (mid to low, high to mid, high to low) are observed. A few rising-falling and falling-rising tones occur also. But they are relatively rare except the possessive suffix of first person singular /-nà'`/ 'my', a low-to-mid rising followed by mid-to-low falling. The syllable which bears a falling or rising tone is longer than the syllable with a level tone. Kar: /da/ [da] 'one' /dá'/…

2288.tone: Source (Matsushita 1974: 15) states three level tones H/M/L, six contour tones (MH, LH, LM rising; ML, HM, HL falling), rare rise-fall and fall-rise (the 1sg possessive suffix /-nà'`/ 'my' bears LM rise + ML fall), and that contour-bearing syllables are longer; it says nothing about stress or accent. Matsushita 1972 (Japanese tone-method note, p. 3, read by B): '/MH-/ の部分の Pitch の上昇はわずかであり, しかも最初の音節は弱めに発音されるので, 容易に */HH-/ と混同してしまった' = 'the pitch rise of the /MH-/ part is slight, and moreover the first syllable is pronounced rather weakly, so it was easily confused with */HH-/' -- a phonetic aside explaining the author's earlier mis-analysis of /MH-MM/ as */HH-LL/, not a stress rule. Newman 1985: 233: 'Gwandara has three tone levels: Hi á, Lo à, and Mid ā... Gwandara does not have distinctive vowel length.' Mustapha & Ishaku 2020: 94 (p. 94; verified) quote Mustapha 2013: 44: 'Gwandara (being a tonal language) can be seen as a syllable-timed language, just like many other African languages' -- no stress placement claim. Verdict is 'tone language, no stress rule described'; no source explicitly denies word stress, so no word stress is not claimed.

2290.tone: Register tone: H, L and a contrastive falling (contour) tone; mora = TBU; eight melodies (HL, LH, L, H, FH, FL, LF, HF) lexically distributed per word; 'all Lugwere tones are contrastive' with lexical (minimal pairs p. 35), grammatical (Hesternal vs Remote past; declarative vs polar question) and discourse functions. The words 'stress' and 'accent' occur nowhere in the 50 pages (a full-text search: only 'prominent syllable pattern' = CV as the commonest syllable type, p. 22). Penult-related facts are phonetic only: half-lengthening of a penultimate vowel bearing a contour tone ('Penult contour tone protraction', p. 13, fn. 1: 'Occurs in all penultimate contour tone contexts except in diphthongs') and, in inflected plural-subject verbs, a root-initial H that 'eventually spreads till the penultimate mora' (p. 33-34). Kagaya 2006 (A Gwere Vocabulary, ILCAA, 'Note of the Gwere Language' pp. iii-ix) likewise has no 'stress'; its 'accent syllable' is the syllable 'where the first tone of each TM associates' (tone melodies H, HL, L), i.e. a tonal docking site, and it notes a vowel before NC 'is definitely long when... placed on the penultimate syllable of a word'.

2296.tone: Coburn 2024 (the only systematic tonal study, 2022 fieldwork): two underlying tones H and L on moras; LH rising much commoner than HL falling, both only on long vowels; toneless suffixes/enclitics get polar tone; automatic downstep (/sésèmé/ 'lion' -> [sésèmē]); lexical minimal pairs e.g. /t͡ʃʰí/ 'run' vs /t͡ʃʰì/ 'capture'; functional load of tone in roots low; all H/L combinations attested on 1-3-syllable noun roots (Sands 2013d:89, reproduced p. 170). Stress: 'this thesis does not find stress in Hadza' (p. 158); earlier 'stress shift' (Sands 2013b:117) reanalysed as morphological vowel lengthening; conclusion p. 211 characterises earlier literature as describing 'numerous tone levels and contours, in addition to some kind of stress'. Earlier sources (per Coburn pp. 165-170 and read directly for Sands et al. 1996/1993): Obst 1912 one acute accent per word, Bleek 1939 'variable stress', Berger 1943 stronger/weaker dynamic accents, Tucker et al. 1977 four level + two contour tones plus 'Stress' (tentative), de Voogt 1992:14 primary stress with free/contextual variation and tone not 'phonologically significant', Sands et al. 1996:178 pitch-accent suggestion with LHL/HL melodies, Miller 2011 H/M/L with pitch-stress correlation.

2302.prule: Morphological (stem) stress: the stem syllable, i.e. the rightmost morpheme and normally the final syllable of the word in this prefixing language, bears prominence ('morphological stress' / 'stem stress'), realised most regularly as longer stem-onset consonants and stem vowels (stem /ə/ 324.3 ms vs unstressed prefix /ə/ 79.2 ms, p < 0.001, p. 77); prefixes are unstressed at the morphological level, and stems cannot take additional word-level rhythmic stress (p. 77). The rule is tied to the morpheme, not to syllable weight or syllable count.
2302.srule: Manker 2012 describes, impressionistically, a word-level 'rhythmic (syllable) stress' separate from stem stress: it tends to fall on the penultimate syllable (the last prefix before the stem) when that syllable has a full vowel, lengthening the vowel to near stem-vowel duration; antepenultimate prefixes and reduced /ə/ prefixes do not take it, and stems take no rhythmic stress on top of stem stress, so full-vowel disyllables sound almost equally stressed on both syllables (pp. 77, 82-83, 89). The author does not rank the two stresses ('unclear which syllables are expected to receive primary and secondary stress', p. 101); Lehman 2020 assumes no secondary stress.

2306.tone: Every modern first-hand source treats Kihehe as a tone language and none states a stress rule. Odden 1988 (c. p.238, excerpt grade): 'Kihehe allows multiple H tones per word' and 'has the nominal tone patterns PSI, PSI plus PU, PU, stem initial, stem initial and final, PSI plus APU, and APU' (PSI = pre-stem-initial, PU = penult, APU = antepenult), with stem-initial H retracting to the pre-stem vowel in definable cases; Odden 2005 (excerpt): rule assigning H to a penultimate vowel not immediately preceded by H (no H in kú-kam-a). Ngwasi 2021 pp.48-49 (open text): lexical minimal pair gúla 'that' vs gula 'buy' (after Kindole 2012); future tense marked solely by penult H, tulíma vs kulima (after Odden & Odden 1999:432). Velten's 1899 'Wortton auf der ersten Stammsilbe' is read here as the stem-initial H pattern heard as prominence: the 'Abweichungen' he marks on the same page 167 (mŭ́goda, mŭ́tima, múnego = accent on the class prefix; mŭtēguló = final; kirongózi, mulagússi = penult) are exactly Odden's PSI, final and PU patterns, so Velten's accents record lexically variable H placement, not a stress rule. His 'accented vowel is long' remark conflicts with the contrastive vowel length of the modern descriptions (5 short + 5 long vowels, Haonga 2022 after Odden & Odden 1999) and is not corroborated. The 'stress' Ngenzi 2022/2023 describe is Swahili penult prominence in L2 speech, not a Kihehe rule.

2309.prule: One prominent syllable per word. Default stress is a left-aligned, quantity-sensitive iamb: the initial syllable if it is heavy (´H), otherwise the second syllable (L´L, L´H). Boyle et al. 2016 (as quoted by Rivera p.4 and Kasak 2024) state the same rule as: primary stress on the second syllable unless the initial syllable is heavy, or the third syllable is heavy and the first two are light. Rivera 2017: 779 of 861 trisyllabic roots (90%) follow the default; 32 roots accent an initial light syllable (Class II), 39 accent the mora right of the initial iamb (Class III).

2309.tone: Rivera 2017: the accented mora always carries the one high tone (H) of the word; F0 (+17 Hz) and amplitude (+1.7 dB) cue it in the default class, duration not significant; H does not spread from the left word edge, contra Park 2012:38 (as quoted p.3: lexical word-level pitch accent with H spreading rightward to the accented mora, L after it). Rivera nonetheless labels the system 'a lexical word-level pitch accent as stated in Park (2012)' because F0 is a cue and Classes II/III deviate from the default iamb (p.27-28). Boyle et al. 2024 sec.2.3 call it stress, say Park's pitch-accent claims were 'shown... to be erroneous' by Rivera 2017 and Metzler 2021, and treat the syllable where intensity and pitch align as stressed. No tone contrasts independent of the single accent are reported by any source in the copy consulted.
